passage: Come, Deepak, sit by your Darshan Dada. You want to know how to help your friend? Let me tell you about Suresh. We were twenty, sharing a room in the college hostel, when his father's shop burned down. Suresh stopped going to class and lay facing the wall. I wanted to give him speeches. I even started to say, "When my mother died, I..." and stopped, because it wasn't about me. So I did small things. I brought his dinner from the mess. I sat on the floor with my books while he stared at the wall. Every evening I asked, "Walk to the tea stall?" Most days he said no. Some days, yes. After a month I told him, "I'm your friend, not a doctor. There's a doctor at the college clinic who talks with students. I'll come with you." He went. Fifty years later, Suresh still sends me mangoes every summer.

qa.q: What happened to Suresh's father's shop?
qa.a: It burned down.

qa.q: Why did Darshan stop in the middle of saying "When my mother died"?
qa.a: Dada realised that comparing his own pain would make it about himself rather than Suresh, and felt it was the wrong moment.

qa.q: What choice did Dada make after a month?
qa.a: He admitted he was a friend, not a doctor, and offered to go with Suresh to the doctor at the college clinic.

qa.q: What might Dada's quiet company have meant to Suresh?
qa.a: Suresh likely felt he was not alone and not pressured, which made it easier to accept the tea-stall walks and later the clinic.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how he helped a struggling friend he shared a hostel room with by listening, keeping him company and bringing food, not lecturing or comparing pain, and nudging him to a doctor.

passage: Gurleen's own exams started on Monday, and the hostel wifi kept dropping. Still, every night at ten she called her friend Chaitanya in his city three hundred kilometres away, even if only for five minutes. Since he'd failed his second-year paper, he mostly spoke in short, flat sentences. On Wednesday he said, "Everyone else is moving on and I'm stuck." Gurleen felt a sharp flicker of resentment. She had her own paper in nine hours. Then she heard how tired he sounded and let it go. She didn't tell him about her cousin who had failed and bounced back, and she didn't list study tips. She only said, "That sounds really heavy. I'm here." On Thursday she found the number for his college counselling cell and sent it with one line: "I'm not a counsellor, but these people are. Want me to stay on the call while you book?" He did. The booking took four minutes.

qa.q: At what time did Gurleen call Chaitanya every night?
qa.a: At ten.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen feel a flicker of resentment on Wednesday?
qa.a: Her own paper was in nine hours, and she was tired and stretched by giving time she needed.

qa.q: What choice did Gurleen make on Thursday, and why was it helpful?
qa.a: She sent the counselling cell's number and offered to stay on the call while Chaitanya booked, a small practical step toward professional help.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt hearing "That sounds really heavy. I'm here" instead of study tips?
qa.a: He may have felt heard rather than judged, which made him more willing to book the counsellor.

grounding: It shows a friend in exam week checking in daily, listening without comparing or lecturing, and giving a small practical nudge toward professional care.

passage: I'm Jomon, and honestly, I didn't see it at first. Rafiq and I have shared a flat since first year. Last spring his school friend Asif went through a terrible breakup, and Rafiq became his everything: calls at two in the morning, skipped classes to sit with him, message after message all day. Then I noticed Rafiq had stopped cooking, stopped playing football, and once fell asleep in the shower. When I asked, he snapped, "If I don't answer and something happens, it's on me." Then he cried, because he also felt guilty for being tired of it. We sat down that night and made a plan. He'd tell Asif, kindly, that he loved him and couldn't be his only person. Asif's brother and the college counsellor would be brought in. Rafiq would keep his phone on silent after midnight unless it was an emergency. It felt harsh to him. It was actually what let him keep helping.

qa.q: What did Rafiq stop doing?
qa.a: Cooking and playing football.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq cry when Jomon asked?
qa.a: He felt guilty for being tired of helping, and afraid that if he didn't answer, anything bad would be his fault.

qa.q: Which part of the plan was hardest for Rafiq, and why was it still a wise choice?
qa.a: Keeping his phone on silent after midnight except in emergencies felt harsh, but it protected his sleep so he could keep helping.

qa.q: What is it like for Rafiq to set these limits?
qa.a: It feels harsh and guilty to him at first, but it gives him rest and shares the load with Asif's brother and the counsellor, so he isn't drained.

grounding: It shows Jomon noticing a young man becoming a friend's only support, drained and guilty, and helping him set kind limits and bring in others.

passage: I'm Omkar. I sit next to Jyoti at the design studio, so I saw most of it, though I can only guess what she felt. From June, she spent every lunch break in the stairwell on the phone, speaking softly: "I know, I know, I'm here." Her friend was going through something bad; that much she told me. By August she was eating biscuits for lunch and her eyes looked puffy most mornings. Once, when her phone buzzed during a client meeting, she went pale and apologised to everyone twice. In September something shifted. I overheard her say, "I care about you, and I can't be the only one. Can I call your mum with you tonight?" After that she took her full lunch break with us. Last Friday she even laughed at the terrible canteen dal. I don't know everything that happened, but she looks like she's breathing again.

qa.q: Where did Jyoti spend every lunch break from June?
qa.a: In the stairwell on the phone.

qa.q: What might Jyoti's pale face during the client meeting suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she may have been anxious that her friend needed her, and embarrassed about the interruption.

qa.q: What choice did Jyoti make in September?
qa.a: She told her friend she cared but couldn't be the only support, and offered to call the friend's mum together.

qa.q: How has the change affected Jyoti, as Omkar sees it?
qa.a: Omkar sees her taking full lunch breaks and laughing again, looking as if she can breathe after months of strain.

grounding: It shows Omkar, who sits beside her at work, watching a young woman drained by being a friend's only support, and seeing her recover once she sets a kind limit and involves others.

passage: Sumit, sit. You look like someone who's been shut out. Let me tell you what happened to me, Zubin, at your age. My closest friend, Behram, lost his place in the university hockey team, and something went out of him. When I knocked on his door, he said, "Just leave me alone, Zubin." I was hurt. Honestly, I was angry. I'd been a good friend! For two days I sulked. Then I wrote him a postcard: "No need to reply. I'm around whenever you want. Chai on me." I sent one every Sunday, nothing heavy. I also asked his mother quietly whether he was safe; she said he was eating and sleeping, just very low. In the fourth month, a postcard came back with one line: "Is the chai offer still open?" If I had kept banging on his door, I think it would have stayed shut.

qa.q: What did Zubin write on the first postcard?
qa.a: No need to reply. I'm around whenever you want. Chai on me.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel when Behram said "leave me alone"?
qa.a: Zubin felt hurt and rejected, even angry, and sulked for two days.

qa.q: Which choice let Zubin respect Behram's pace safely?
qa.a: Zubin quietly asked Behram's mother whether he was safe, and on hearing he was, kept sending gentle weekly postcards instead of pushing.

qa.q: What might the Sunday postcards have meant to Behram in those months?
qa.a: They showed Behram that a friend was still there without demanding anything, so he could come back when he was ready.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling feeling rejected when a friend pushed Zubin away, and keeping the door open with low-pressure messages while checking he was safe.

passage: The monsoon had knocked out power in Damini's hostel for the third evening when her friend Afreen's message finally came: "Please stop checking on me. Just leave me alone." Damini read it by torchlight and felt her face burn. She had called every day since Afreen went home after leaving the course. She typed three angry replies and deleted them all. Instead she wrote, "Okay. I'll stop asking questions. I'm still here whenever you want." After that she sent only small things every few days: a photo of the canteen cat, a song, no questions. Two weeks later, at midnight, Afreen wrote, "Thanks for everything. It won't matter much soon." Damini's stomach dropped. This was different. She phoned Afreen's elder sister at once, then a helpline for advice, and stayed awake until the sister messaged: "I'm with Afreen now. We're going to the doctor."

qa.q: What did Damini send after that first message?
qa.a: Only small things every few days: a photo of the canteen cat, a song, no questions.

qa.q: How did Damini feel reading "leave me alone", and how can you tell?
qa.a: Hurt and rejected, even angry; her face burned and she typed three angry replies before deleting them.

qa.q: Why did Damini change her approach after the midnight message?
qa.a: "It won't matter much soon" sounded like danger, so waiting was no longer right; she phoned Afreen's sister and a helpline at once.

qa.q: How might Afreen have seen the no-questions messages?
qa.a: They may have felt safe and unpressured, keeping a door open with a friend while Afreen had no energy to talk.

grounding: It shows a friend who feels rejected when told to leave someone alone, stays gently reachable at their pace, and acts at once when a message sounds like danger.

subtype: Adult child seeing a parent low or anxious [Actor]
passage: Yusuf, I heard you on the phone with your father just now. Can I tell you something from my own life? When I was about your age, my Appa retired and then just faded. He stopped reading the newspaper. He sat on the balcony till dark and barely spoke at meals. I was the one living at home, so I quietly took over: the bills, his tablets, the cooking, even reminding him to bathe. I felt I had become his parent, and I was frightened and guilty all the time, because I was angry too. My brothers in the city had no idea. One night I finally phoned them and said, "I can't do this alone." That weekend all three of us sat with Appa and said, "We love you. You don't seem yourself. Let's see Dr Rao together." He grumbled, but he went. It helped him, slowly. And it helped me more than I can say. I'm Uma, and I wish I'd called them sooner.

qa.q: Where did Uma's Appa sit till dark?
qa.a: On the balcony.

qa.q: What did Uma feel while quietly taking over everything?
qa.a: Uma felt frightened and guilty, and angry too, as if Uma had become Appa's parent.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Uma?
qa.a: Phoning the brothers and saying "I can't do this alone", which led all three to speak lovingly with Appa and take him to Dr Rao.

qa.q: How might Appa have felt when all three children sat with him?
qa.a: He may have felt embarrassed, hence the grumbling, but also loved and less alone, which is why he agreed to go.

grounding: It shows an older person recalling seeing a father withdraw, feeling role reversal, fear and guilt, and choosing to share the load with siblings and suggest a doctor.

subtype: Adult child seeing a parent low or anxious [Actor]
passage: Ammi called Parveen four times before noon, as she did most days now. Had Parveen reached work? Was the gas off at home? Had Nadeem's train arrived safely? On the crowded station platform, Parveen could barely hear her over the announcements. Ammi's voice was thin and fast, and she said she hadn't slept properly since Abbu's operation. Parveen felt her chest tighten. Somewhere in the last year she had started parenting her own mother, and it frightened her. She also felt guilty for being irritated by the calls. That night she texted her brother Nadeem: "Ammi isn't okay. I've been handling it alone and I can't. Can we both talk to her on Sunday?" On Sunday, squeezed onto Ammi's bed, they held her hands. "Ammi, we love you. This much worry is hard on your health. Will you come with us to Dr Mathew?" Ammi cried, then nodded. Nadeem booked the visit; Parveen promised to come too.

qa.q: How many times did Ammi call before noon?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What two feelings did Parveen have about Ammi's calls?
qa.a: Fear at having started to parent her own mother, and guilt at feeling irritated by the calls.

qa.q: Which choice changed things, and why?
qa.a: Parveen stopped handling it alone and asked Nadeem to talk to Ammi together, so the load was shared and Ammi was gently steered to a doctor.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel when both children held her hands?
qa.a: She may feel loved and seen rather than scolded, which is why she cried and then agreed to see Dr Mathew.

grounding: It shows a young woman seeing her mother constantly worried, feeling role reversal, fear and guilt, and speaking with love and her brother to suggest a doctor visit.

passage: In the kitchen of her mother's house in Durban, Noa watched Lindiwe stir the same pot of stew long after it was cooked. For months her mother had barely left the house, skipped choir and stopped answering her sister's calls. When Noa gently mentioned a counsellor, Lindiwe set the spoon down hard. "I'm fine. I'm not some weak woman who needs to cry to a stranger. And what would the neighbours say?" Noa felt the door close. She didn't argue. A week later she tried again, differently. "Ma, you see Dr Pillay every year for your blood pressure. Sleep and mood are health too. Would you let him check those at your next visit? I'll drive you, and you decide what you tell him." Lindiwe was quiet for a long time. "Dr Pillay has known me thirty years," she said at last. "Fine. Only him." Noa booked it that evening.

qa.q: What does Lindiwe see Dr Pillay for every year?
qa.a: Her blood pressure.

qa.q: Why did Lindiwe refuse the counsellor at first?
qa.a: She felt it would make her look weak and was worried about what the neighbours would say.

qa.q: What did Noa change in her second attempt?
qa.a: Noa framed it as health, brought in the trusted family doctor, and let Lindiwe decide what to tell him.

qa.q: How did the second approach feel different for Lindiwe?
qa.a: It respected her dignity and her trust in Dr Pillay, so accepting help felt like a check-up rather than an admission of weakness.

grounding: It shows a young woman whose mother insists she is fine and fears gossip and weakness, and who wins acceptance by framing it as health through a trusted family doctor.

passage: In Dr Joseph's waiting room, Swati's father sat with his arms folded, eyes on the door. "I told you, I'm fine," Siddharth muttered. "If anyone from our building sees me here, they'll say the old man has gone soft in the head." For three months he hadn't gone on his morning walk and had barely touched dinner. Swati had tried once already, and he'd said only weak people talk to psychologists. So today she had put it differently. "Papa, Dr Joseph has looked after you since your knee operation. We're here because you're not sleeping. Sleep is health, same as your knee." He grunted. When his name was called, Swati stood too, then sat back down. "Do you want me in there, or would you like to talk to her alone?" Siddharth hesitated. "Alone," he said, and straightened his collar before going in.

qa.q: What hadn't Siddharth done for three months?
qa.a: Gone on his morning walk.

qa.q: What was Siddharth worried about in the waiting room?
qa.a: That someone from the building would see him and say he had gone soft in the head.

qa.q: Which choice by Swati protected her father's dignity?
qa.a: She asked whether he wanted her in the room or to talk to Dr Joseph alone, and let him decide.

qa.q: What might Siddharth's straightening his collar suggest about how he felt going in?
qa.a: It suggests he wanted to walk in with self-respect, feeling that the choice was his own.

grounding: It shows a daughter whose older father resists help out of fear of gossip and weakness, framing it as health with the family doctor and respecting his dignity.

passage:
Home-visit notes, community nurse, Thursday.
Visited Mr Dave, bedridden since spring. His daughter Hansa has been the main carer. Last month she looked grey with tiredness and said she hadn't slept a full night in weeks. Today there was a change. Her son Jagdish, who works in the city, has made a chart on the fridge: who does night turns, who cooks, who handles medicines, with his sister and a cousin on it too. He asked me directly whether Hansa was eating properly and whether the bathroom was safe for her at night. He admitted he had skipped his own badminton for a month and was getting snappy. We agreed he would keep Wednesday evenings for himself.
What I did next: I gave the family the number of the carers' support group, and booked a doctor's check-up for Hansa next week.

qa.q: What did Jagdish put on the fridge?
qa.a: A chart: who does night turns, who cooks, who handles medicines.

qa.q: How had Hansa been feeling last month, and what showed it?
qa.a: Exhausted; she looked grey with tiredness and said she hadn't slept a full night in weeks.

qa.q: Why was keeping Wednesday evenings for himself a wise choice for Jagdish?
qa.a: He had skipped badminton and was getting snappy; protecting some time for himself guards against burnout so he can keep helping.

qa.q: How might Hansa feel seeing her son's chart and questions?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and cared for, no longer carrying every night turn alone.

grounding: It shows a son checking his caregiving mother's sleep, meals and safety, sharing tasks, bringing in professional help and protecting his own time.

passage:
Saturday night.
Came home at seven and found Ma asleep sitting up beside Thakuma's bed, the dinner pot still cold on the stove. I realised I couldn't remember the last time I'd seen her eat lunch. She keeps saying, "Thakuma needs me, I'm fine," but she's snapping at everyone and forgetting her own headache tablets.
So tonight I did three things. I heated the dal and sat with her until she'd eaten it. I called Mashi and asked her to take Sundays with Thakuma; she said yes straight away, sounding almost relieved to be asked. And I booked Ma an appointment with Dr Sen for Tuesday, for the headaches and the tiredness.
I also nearly cancelled my trek with Charu next month. Then I pictured both Ma and me burnt out. I'm keeping it.
Bidisha

qa.q: What did Bidisha find when coming home at seven?
qa.a: Ma asleep sitting up beside Thakuma's bed, the dinner pot still cold on the stove.

qa.q: What worried Bidisha about Ma?
qa.a: Bidisha was worried because Ma was sleeping sitting up, skipping lunch, snapping at everyone and forgetting her own tablets.

qa.q: Why was keeping the trek with Charu a wise choice?
qa.a: Bidisha saw that giving up everything would lead to both Ma and Bidisha burning out, which would help nobody.

qa.q: How might Mashi see being asked to take Sundays?
qa.a: She sounded almost relieved, perhaps glad to be allowed to help instead of watching from the side.

grounding: It shows a young adult checking Ma's meals, sleep and health while Ma cares for Thakuma, sharing tasks with Mashi, booking a doctor and protecting their own life.

passage: In the colony park, the older boys pointed at the man who talked to himself near the gate. "Paagal! Paagal!" they chanted. Sunaina laughed too, then stopped. At night her own worries buzzed like mosquitoes and kept her awake. Would they call her paagal too? She decided never to tell anyone. Irfan Uncle from the second floor had heard the boys. That evening, watering his plants, he said, "That man's mind is unwell, the way a body gets unwell. It isn't funny, and it isn't his fault. I saw a doctor myself when my worries got too big." Sunaina twisted her frock. "Mine buzz at night," she whispered. Irfan Uncle put down the watering can. "Thank you for telling me. Let's go up and tell your Mummy together." They did, and Mummy hugged her and listened.

qa.q: What did the older boys chant?
qa.a: Paagal! Paagal!

qa.q: Why did Sunaina decide never to tell anyone about her night worries?
qa.a: After hearing the boys mock the man, she felt ashamed and feared they would call her paagal too.

qa.q: Which words from Irfan Uncle made it safe for Sunaina to speak?
qa.a: He said an unwell mind is like an unwell body, not funny and not anyone's fault, and that he too saw a doctor when his worries got too big.

qa.q: How might the man near the gate feel hearing the chant?
qa.a: He might feel hurt and ashamed, and less likely to reach out for help.

grounding: It shows a child learning from mockery that struggling is shameful, until an adult speaks openly about minds and health and she shares her own worries.

passage:
"Look at Kunal flapping his hands again. Something's wrong in his head!"
"Stop it. He's just excited about the rocket model."
"Tanuja, why are you taking his side? Are you weird too?"
Tanuja went quiet. She thought of how she checked her school bag five times every morning, and hid her hands under the desk.
Salma Ma'am put down the chalk. "Enough. Everyone's mind works a bit differently. Kunal shows happiness with his hands. Some of us worry a lot. Talking about minds is like talking about a cough. It's health, not a joke."
After the bell, Tanuja lingered. "Ma'am, I check my bag again and again, or I feel scared. Is something wrong in my head?"
"Thank you for telling me, Tanuja. It's nothing to be ashamed of. Shall we tell your mother together at pickup today?"
Tanuja nodded, and her shoulders came down a little.

qa.q: What was Kunal excited about?
qa.a: The rocket model.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja hide her hands under the desk?
qa.a: After hearing Kunal mocked, she felt ashamed and afraid that her own habit of checking her bag would make her seem weird too.

qa.q: Which choice by Salma Ma'am helped Tanuja most after the bell?
qa.a: She thanked Tanuja, said it was nothing to be ashamed of, and offered to tell Tanuja's mother together at pickup that day.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel hearing Salma Ma'am say he shows happiness with his hands?
qa.a: He may feel understood and protected instead of laughed at.

grounding: It shows a child who hears a classmate with a difference mocked and starts hiding her own worries, until a teacher talks about minds as health and listens.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 11, Friday.
Dolma has come to Thursday sessions for two months. Her parents support it, but have asked her to tell relatives she is at "extra maths", because an aunt keeps worrying aloud about what people will say, with her elder sister's marriage talks going on. Dolma says the lie itself is exhausting. At lunch she sits alone so no one asks where she goes on Thursdays, and she says she feels as if she's living behind glass.
Today we made a list of people she might trust. She chose one: her lab partner Abhinav, who once mentioned his own brother's counselling. What I did next: we practised what she might say, and she agreed I could check in. She came back after lunch looking lighter. "He just said thanks for telling him, and asked if I want company on Thursdays," she said. She smiled for most of the session.

qa.q: What have Dolma's parents asked her to tell relatives?
qa.a: That she is at "extra maths".

qa.q: How does Dolma feel about keeping the secret?
qa.a: Lonely and exhausted, as if living behind glass.

qa.q: What step did the counsellor help Dolma take?
qa.a: Choosing one trusted person, Abhinav, and practising what to say before telling him.

qa.q: How might Abhinav see Dolma's news, given his own brother's counselling?
qa.a: He likely sees it as ordinary and nothing to be ashamed of, which is why he thanked her and offered company on Thursdays.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose family hides her counselling out of fear of gossip and marriage worries, whose secrecy brings loneliness, and who feels relief telling a trusted person.

passage:
Sunday, after Pinky Didi's wedding.
Everyone kept asking why I'd missed so much school this term. Mummy answered for me every time: "Typhoid, poor thing." It wasn't typhoid. The doctor gave what I have a name months ago, and I see a psychologist every week. But Mummy says if anyone finds out, the whole family will talk, and Didi's in-laws might think something runs in our family. So I smiled and lied all day, and felt like the loneliest person in a hall of four hundred people.
Then my cousin Chaitanya found me on the back steps. He said, "You don't have to tell me anything. You just look tired." I told him. Not the name, just that I'm getting help. He said, "Okay. I'm glad you are." That's all. No fuss.
For the first time all day, my chest unknotted. Maybe I get to choose who knows.
Kamal

qa.q: What did Mummy tell people every time?
qa.a: Typhoid, poor thing.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel at the wedding, and why?
qa.a: Kamal felt like the loneliest person in a hall of four hundred people, because of smiling and lying all day to hide the truth.

qa.q: What choice on the back steps changed Kamal's day?
qa.a: Kamal chose to tell one trusted person, Chaitanya, only as much as felt right, and felt relief.

qa.q: Why might Mummy feel the need to hide it?
qa.a: She fears the family's gossip and that Didi's in-laws might judge, so hiding feels like protection to her.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose family conceals a diagnosis to avoid gossip and marriage worries, and how secrecy brings loneliness while choosing a trusted cousin brings relief.

passage: At the college canteen, Chandrika lined up her highlighters by colour and announced, "Sorry, I'm so OCD." Everyone laughed. Then someone said the new maths lecturer was "totally mental" for springing a surprise test, and the laughter got louder. Sumit noticed Faisal, at the end of the table, go very still and stare into his tea. Sumit took a breath. "Can I say something without being annoying? People who actually live with OCD describe it as exhausting, not neat pens. And calling the lecturer 'mental', maybe let's not." Chandrika went red. "Oh. I didn't think. Sorry." The table was awkward for a second, then someone asked about the test and the talk moved on. That evening Faisal messaged Sumit: "Thanks for saying that. I've been seeing a counsellor for a while. I never felt I could say it in that group."

qa.q: What did Chandrika line up by colour?
qa.a: Chandrika's highlighters.

qa.q: What did Faisal's stillness suggest to Sumit?
qa.a: Sumit sensed that Faisal felt hurt or uncomfortable, perhaps because the jokes touched something personal.

qa.q: Which choice by Sumit changed the table's tone?
qa.a: Sumit asked to speak, briefly said what living with OCD is really like, and asked them to drop "mental", without shaming Chandrika.

qa.q: How did Sumit's words affect Faisal?
qa.a: Faisal felt safe enough to tell Sumit he was seeing a counsellor, something he had never felt able to say in that group.

grounding: It shows a peer who notices how casual jokes about OCD and being mental hurt someone at the table, gently corrects them, and makes it safer for that person to speak.

passage:
"Ugh, Manav is so bipolar today. Happy at ten, grumpy by eleven," Kashish said, dropping into the chair by the printer.
Tarun kept his voice easy. "Maybe just moody? Bipolar is a real illness. People live with it for years."
"Relax, it's just a word."
"I know you don't mean it badly. But words like that land on someone. Half this floor could be dealing with things we'd never guess."
Kashish rolled her eyes, then paused. "Fine. Moody. Happy now?"
"Very," Tarun said, grinning.
Two weeks later, at the team lunch, Arpit groaned, "This client is a total psycho."
Before Tarun could speak, Kashish said, "Call him difficult. Psycho's not a joke word."
Arpit shrugged. "Okay. Difficult."
Across the table, the quiet new intern looked up and, for the first time, joined the conversation.

qa.q: What word did Tarun suggest instead of "bipolar"?
qa.a: Moody.

qa.q: Why did Tarun keep his voice easy when correcting Kashish?
qa.a: He wanted to point out the harm without making her feel attacked, hoping she would listen rather than get defensive.

qa.q: Which part of Tarun's approach made Kashish willing to change?
qa.a: He stayed relaxed, said he knew she didn't mean it badly, and offered a simple alternative word.

qa.q: How did Kashish's view change by the team lunch?
qa.a: Kashish went from calling it "just a word" to correcting Arpit herself, showing she now saw how such words can hurt.

grounding: It shows a young worker who hears illness words used as casual jokes, corrects them gently, and sees the team's way of speaking change.

passage: I'm Ganga. I sit two desks from Salma at the accounts office, and I've watched her do something I didn't know was possible. When Mohan said he was leaving early for physio, Salma said, just as easily, "I'm off at five too, therapy day." No drama. When Hemant pushed, "Therapy for what?", she smiled and said, "That's mine to keep, but it helps." I think it cost her something, though I can't be sure. Last month our new trainee, Varsha, cried in the washroom after a bad review. Salma didn't say "poor thing". She sat down beside her and said, "Rough day. Want some water? If it keeps feeling heavy, our company counsellor is good." Since then, two people have mentioned their own counselling at lunch as if it were a dentist visit. I don't know if Salma planned that. I just know the room feels different.

qa.q: What did Salma say when Hemant asked "Therapy for what?"
qa.a: That's mine to keep, but it helps.

qa.q: What does Ganga think about how Salma felt when speaking openly?

Diwali, Saturday. At Masi's house, Leela's cousin Sudha barely touched the sweets and said, "I don't know what's wrong with me. I just can't feel anything lately." Leela almost mentioned her own year of therapy, then held back. Too many aunts nearby, and she wasn't ready to say it in a crowd.
The next Thursday. Leela took Sudha for a walk by the lake. "Two years ago I had a really dark stretch," she said. "I saw a psychologist for eight months, the same way I saw a physio after I broke my ankle. It helped." She didn't say "poor you". She asked, "Do you want the name of someone good?"
Three weeks later. A message from Sudha: "Went for my second session. Also told my roommate. She said she's been wanting to go too. Thanks for saying it out loud, Leela."

qa.q: Where did Leela take Sudha the next Thursday?
qa.a: For a walk by the lake.

qa.q: Why did Leela hold back at Masi's house?
qa.a: Too many aunts were nearby, and she felt uneasy and not ready to say it in a crowd.

qa.q: What choice did Leela make on the walk, and why did it work?
qa.a: She shared her own therapy plainly, like physio for an ankle, and offered a name instead of pity, which made help feel normal.

qa.q: How has Leela's openness reached Sudha's roommate?
qa.a: Hearing Sudha talk about it, the roommate admitted wanting to go too, so one honest talk made it easier for the next person.

grounding: It shows a young woman sharing her own therapy only when comfortable, treating it like physical care, supporting her cousin without pity, and the openness spreading.
